title: Operationalizing the Structure-Preserving Translation Method: A Preliminary Audit of Genki Theory and Koku Universe Theory
summary: This technical note operationalizes a proposed Structure-Preserving Translation Method (SPTM) for auditing translations between scientific models and metaphysical hypothesis systems. It provides a deliberately limited reference implementation for finite-dimensional linear systems, unit tests, seven synthetic calibration cases, machine-readable results, a preregistration draft, and a preliminary application to Genki Theory and Koku Universe Theory. The synthetic calibration achieved 4 true positives, 3 true negatives, 0 false positives, and 0 false negatives; these developer-constructed cases demonstrate internal implementation behavior only and do not establish external validity. The method remains a validation-ready candidate pending preregistered external benchmarks, blinded assessment, and independent replication. The application does not prove the physical existence of KOKU, GENKI, Koku-density, Ma, I-gen, a hidden universe, mind-energy, prophecy, or reactionless propulsion. A force-only KOKU-DRIVE representation fails the audit because it omits the reaction degree of freedom. A conservation-complete device-plus-field representation is classified only as a testable-surplus candidate and requires an independently measurable field observable.

title: Financial Attrition and Structural Reform in a Hyper-Strong Dollar Environment Critique of Anglo-Saxon Interventionism, Semiconductor Supply Chain Relocation to Japan, and a Simultaneous Resolution Model for China's External Liquidity, Employment, and Asset Privatization via the 170 JPY/USD Catalyst
summary: This paper mathematically models and empirically validates the macro-financial and geopolitical impacts of an extreme US dollar appreciation against the Japanese yen—specifically targeting a critical threshold of 170 JPY/USD. It demonstrates how this exchange rate operates as a "financial attrition" mechanism that restricts foreign currency (USD) liquidity in non-liberal regimes, ultimately forcing structural economic reform in China through the privatization and legal protection of coastal real estate assets, while simultaneously mitigating its domestic youth unemployment crisis. The core theoretical contribution of this study lies in exposing the internal logical contradiction (ideological hypocrisy) of Anglo-Saxon (US/UK) monetary interventionism and "dealer" discretion when evaluated against their own institutional norms of free-market capitalism and the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH). Driven by an asymmetric monetary policy alignment—Federal Reserve rate hikes induced by sticky US inflation versus Bank of Japan policy rate freezes justified by stable, moderate domestic inflation—alongside the strategic relocation of semiconductor Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) to Japan, 170 JPY/USD is established as an equilibrium threshold. This paper concludes with a neutral fiscal buffer model for Japan to absorb imported inflation, demonstrating a sustainable framework that integrates China into the Western rule-of-law framework through pure market mechanics.

title: Do good, get paid: an analysis of the social bond market
summary: Abstract We analyze the niche market for social bonds and empirically investigate the existence of a negative social bond premium. Using a bond matching method, we compare the i-spreads of 280 social bonds over a one-year period with those of their conventional counterparts, resulting in 50,465 observations for social bonds and 100,930 for conventional bonds. Additionally, we examine the influence of specific bond and issuer characteristics, as well as time variables, on the negative premium. Our results indicate that social bonds trade marginally tighter than conventional bonds, with a smaller issue size and slightly higher volatility. Further analysis shows that ESG assurance, region, and timing impact the negative premium. Over time, the negative premium diminishes, which may be due to shifts in capital away from sustainable investments.

title: Pengaruh Transformasi Digital dan Green Accounting Terhadap Kinerja Keuangan Sektor Energi
summary: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis dampak transformasi digital dan green accounting terhadap kinerja keuangan perusahaan-perusahaan sektor energi yang terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia untuk periode 2021–2025. Dengan menggunakan metode kuantitatif dan teknik pengambilan sampel purposif, dipilih 17 perusahaan sebagai sampel (79 pengamatan data setelah penyaringan nilai-nilai outlier dan autokorelasi). Data dianalisis menggunakan regresi linier berganda melalui perangkat lunak SPSS versi 30. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan bahwa, secara individual, transformasi digital dan green accounting memiliki pengaruh positif dan signifikan terhadap Return on Assets (ROA). Secara kolektif, kedua variabel ini juga memiliki pengaruh yang signifikan terhadap profitabilitas keuangan, dengan nilai R-Square yang Disesuaikan sebesar 39,0 persen. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa sinergi antara investasi dalam teknologi informasi dan pengungkapan biaya lingkungan dapat memperkuat legitimasi sosial dan keunggulan kompetitif perusahaan dalam jangka panjang.

title: Sustainable tourism intermediation: a ten-point management guide for the responsible marketing of destinations
summary: The aim of this work is to propose a ten-point business management framework that facilitates the effective integration of sustainability into the marketing of tourist destinations through intermediaries. The methodology adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and propositional approach, based on a narrative review of the literature on tourism intermediation, sustainable management, supply chain, digitalization, consumer behavior, and environmental communication, complemented by an intentional analysis of best practices developed by national and international operators. The evidence obtained was organized through thematic analysis and transformed into ten operational principles related to business strategy, supplier selection, product design, impact reduction, digitalization, training, transparency, local participation, demand orientation, and continuous evaluation. The main result of the research is the proposal of a ten-point framework for integrating sustainability into the marketing of destinations through tourism intermediaries. It is concluded that sustainability acquires a strategic character when it transcends the internal sphere of the company and extends to the supply chain, product design, and marketing. The ten principles constitute a flexible and transferable tool, although its application will need to be validated later in diverse tourism companies and contexts.

title: Creating Digital Sustainable Business Models in Cluster‐Based Energy Ecosystems
summary: ABSTRACT Overlapping economic, social, sustainable, health, and military crises create new spaces for scientific research to be applied to practice. The paper focuses on constructing and configuring digital sustainable business models for energy ecosystems that can effectively respond to and mitigate the impacts of dynamic climate change. This topic is important as it contributes to the global transition toward resilient and resource‐efficient energy systems. The research builds on established concepts in strategic management, digital transformation, and sustainability‐oriented business modeling. It also draws on prior studies linking regional innovation ecosystems, public–private collaboration, and energy transition governance. By connecting these strands, the paper extends existing discussions surrounding digital and sustainable innovation in regional energy networks. A qualitative research design was employed to analyze the mechanisms that enable or hinder the creation and management of digital sustainable business models. The findings reveal central barriers and enablers for effectively and efficiently managing digital sustainable business models in energy ecosystems. Among others, coordination complexity, data integration, and regulatory fragmentation were identified as critical barriers, while collaborative governance structures and digital platforms act as strong enablers. The main contribution is the integration of digital transformation and sustainability logic within business model research applied to regional energy ecosystems. It delivers original insights into how digital sustainable business models can be structured to enhance climate resilience and offers a holistic understanding of ecosystem governance under crisis conditions. The thorough qualitative foundation supports both theoretical advancement and practical policy orientation.

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Predicting Indonesian Vocational School Accreditation: Geographic Validation, Probability Calibration, and Subgroup Auditing
summary: Vocational school accreditation is a high-stakes institutional classification, yet the geographic transferability and probability reliability of models based on routinely collected administrative data remain underexplored. This study developed a reproducible, leakage-controlled machine-learning framework for classifying the recorded accreditation classes C, B, and A among Indonesian vocational schools. Its main contribution is an integrated evaluation design that combines province-disjoint validation, probability calibration, cluster-aware uncertainty, and subgroup auditing to test reliability beyond conventional random-validation performance. A cross-sectional dataset containing 149,376 program-level records was deterministically aggregated into 14,391 schools, including 14,134 with valid labels. Eight provinces comprising 1,536 schools were locked before feature selection, model comparison, tuning, and calibration; 12,598 schools from 31 provinces supported development. The selected CatBoost model used 35 structural and vocational features with grouped out-of-fold temperature scaling. On the locked holdout, the calibrated model achieved balanced accuracy of 0.586, Macro F1 of 0.533, quadratic weighted kappa of 0.499, Macro ROC-AUC of 0.757, and expected calibration error of 0.049. School size, teacher resources, vocational staffing, program diversity, and status were most in-fluential. Class B had the lowest recall, and performance varied across school groups and provinces. The framework supports calibrated, auditable preliminary screening, but not automated accreditation or replacement of professional assessors.

title: The role of Islamic crowdfunding in supporting environmental sustainability goals: insights from Indonesia’s Sharia-based securities crowdfunding platforms
summary: Purpose The presence of the Islamic finance industry offers new opportunities for aligning ethical and responsible investment with worldwide sustainability objectives. In Indonesia, Sharia-based securities crowdfunding (SBSC) is an emerging equity-based crowdfunding platform that has the potential to become a funding alternative for environmentally friendly initiatives in the business sector. Thus, this study aims to explore the extent to which the platform supports the achievement of environmental sustainability goals. Design/methodology/approach This study uses an exploratory qualitative design through semi-structured interviews with key practitioners from three SBSC platforms. To ensure data triangulation, the interview transcripts are complemented by a systematic review of institutional publications collected from their official websites. The consolidated data were analyzed using NVivo-based thematic analysis to identify emerging patterns and strategic implications. Findings This study reveals a growing awareness among SBSC platforms of sectors aligned with environmental sustainability goals. Nonetheless, platform support and initiatives toward environmental sustainability are still limited and varied among the SBSC platforms. This is primarily due to the lack of formalized policies, underdeveloped institutional mechanisms and the absence of regulatory drivers. Research limitations/implications This study is limited to three SBSC platforms focusing on their activities concerning environmental sustainability within the 2021–2024 period. The findings imply the need for platform transition and institutional reform toward more environmentally conscious operations, alongside a formal sustainability-related policy framework at regulatory level. Practical implications The findings highlight the need for structured sustainability screening, environmental disclosure, monitoring and reporting mechanisms grounded in Islamic principles. Strengthening these mechanisms may improve governance and accountability and support the institutionalization of environmental sustainability within the Islamic crowdfunding ecosystem. Social implications This study highlights the broader societal relevance of SBSC platforms in promoting environmental sustainability through Islamic finance. Integrating sustainability considerations may expand access to sustainable finance, raise environmental awareness among market participants, and strengthen alignment between financial activities, Islamic ethical values and environmental sustainability objectives. Originality/value This study provides one of the first empirical investigations into how SBSC platforms operationalize environmental sustainability within their platform-level practices. In doing so, it extends the Islamic crowdfunding literature by providing empirical evidence on the institutional processes through which environmental sustainability is translated into practice.

title: Mapping knowledge structures, research concentration, and governance visibility in technology-related sustainable tourism research
summary: Abstract This study maps the knowledge structures, research concentration, collaboration patterns, and governance visibility of technology-related sustainable tourism research. The analysis draws on 1,044 Scopus-indexed publications issued between 2010 and 2023 and applies bibliometric performance analysis and science-mapping techniques using VOSviewer. Publication growth, country and author co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and the occurrence and connectivity of governance- and evaluation-related terms were examined. A retrospective source-type audit and a sensitivity analysis based on a conservative journal-only subset (n = 611) were also conducted to assess the robustness of the findings. The results reveal rapid publication growth after 2020 and a prominent sustainability-technology core centred on sustainable development, smart tourism, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, big data, and digital transformation. Publication output, citation visibility, and collaboration were concentrated within a limited group of countries and author communities. Governance- and evaluation-related terms were identifiable but remained less prominent and less connected than the dominant sustainability and technology concepts. The sensitivity analysis confirmed the stability of the principal patterns: the annual publication trends were nearly identical (r = 0.999), while nine of the ten leading countries and 18 of the 20 leading keywords were retained. The study contributes a diagnostic framework that combines knowledge structure, research concentration, and governance visibility to assess how technological sustainability claims are organised within tourism scholarship.

title: Species-independent estimation of dipterocarp wood density using drilling resistance: implications for carbon accounting
summary: Nature-based carbon credit markets are crucial for climate change mitigation in tropical regions. Accurate estimates of aboveground biomass (AGB) in these forests depend on wood density (WD), typically sourced from global databases that do not account for local variability, introducing substantial uncertainties in carbon stock assessments. This study evaluates the resistograph as a novel tool for improving WD predictions in dipterocarp forests of northern Borneo, addressing critical gaps in current carbon stock estimation methodologies. Using multiple linear regression, we developed a two-variable model linking WD to drilling resistance (DR) variables. The optimal model, incorporating the standard deviation of DR (DRStD) and the slope of DR (DRSlope), produced the best predictions (adjusted R² = 0.604, RMSE = 0.083 g cm-3) and showed no significant difference from field WD. Log-transformed models were also tested as a robustness check and yielded lower prediction errors, but the final model was selected for its higher explanatory power and direct interpretability. By comparison, database WD values significantly overestimated field WD and resulted in inflated AGB estimates (RMSE = 32.260%) compared to those derived from the resistograph-based model (RMSE = 25.933%). Our findings demonstrate that the resistograph-based methodology accurately predicts field WD. As a non-destructive and portable tool, it has large potential to enhance the credibility of biomass quantification for nature-based carbon credit projects in Southeast Asia. Further work should expand geographical and species coverage to support broader application across tropical forest landscapes.

title: Artificial intelligence and environmental auditing toward sustainable risk management: the complex moderating roles of ethical leadership and perceived greenwashing
summary: Purpose Drawing on dynamic capability and agency theories, this study aims to examine how artificial intelligence capacity (AICA) influences sustainable risk management (SURM) through environmental audit effectiveness (EAEF) and how perceived greenwashing (PGWA) and ethical leadership (ETLE) jointly shape this relationship. Design/methodology/approach A moderated moderation and mediation model was tested using survey data from chief financial officers in Vietnam’s manufacturing sector. Findings AICA significantly improves EAEF, which in turn enhances SURM, confirming EAEF’s mediating role. PGWA positively moderates the AICA–EAEF relationship, and this effect is further strengthened by ETLE. Research limitations/implications The findings extend dynamic capability and agency theories by conceptualizing AICA and EAEF as dynamic capabilities and positioning PGWA and ETLE as governance mechanisms that mitigate agency problems in sustainability reporting. Practical implications The study highlights the importance of AI adoption, ETLE and regulatory enforcement in improving audit quality, transparency and reducing greenwashing. Originality/value This study introduces a moderated moderation model showing how PGWA and ETLE jointly strengthen the AICA–EAEF relationship. By framing them as complementary governance mechanisms rather than independent antecedents, it advances research on technology-enabled sustainability governance.

title: Capacity development approaches and strategies in climate change adaptation projects in Latin America: A typology
summary: The success of climate adaptation projects globally is dependent upon a multitude of factors, including the various actions which are designed into a project, as well as more contextual factors affecting the delivery of those actions. Capacity development, sometimes referred to as capacity building, is one type of action which has been identified as having the potential to improve the delivery of a project but perhaps, more importantly, ensure its impact and sustainability beyond the limitations of a project. Using mainland Latin America as a focus region, this paper analyses 60 ‘real world’ climate adaptation project proposals, funded by three different multilateral climate finance mechanisms, in order to highlight the principal characteristics of the capacity development strategies across all projects. Through the manual coding of each proposal, a typology of twelve different ‘types’ of capacity development actions was created, which seeks to outline the specific delivery modality and strategic approach employed by a project, taking into account learning dynamics and possible power relationships. In addition to the typology as an output, findings demonstrate that consideration of capacity development elements remains insufficient across many projects, and that, while there has been movement towards strategies emphasising empowerment, local ownership and long-term change, a significant shift is still required: one which moves away from a reliance upon traditional top-down methods of developing knowledge and coordinating stakeholders, to initiatives which include more participatory, iterative and enabling actions.

title: Interrogating the Comparative Benefits of Nationalisation and Privatisation of Mines in Zambia: A Case of Chingola and Mufulira Districts
summary: Zambia’s Copperbelt province has experienced changing approaches to copper mining governance, shifting from state ownership to privatisation and, more recently, to hybrid arrangements. This article comparatively examines nationalisation and privatisation through case studies of Chingola, home to Konkola Copper Mines (KCM), and Mufulira, home to Mopani Copper Mines (MCM). Drawing on Dependency Theory, the Obsolescing Bargain Model, Public Choice Theory of privatisation and the Resource Curse Thesis, it traces ownership changes from the 1969 Mulungushi and Matero Declarations, through the 1997–2000 privatisation of Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM), to current arrangements involving Vedanta Resources, ZCCM Investments Holdings (ZCCM-IH) and International Resources Holding (IRH). Using a mixed-methods comparative case study, the study combines questionnaire data from 140 respondents with interviews and documentary analysis. Findings reveal low satisfaction with current ownership across four of five dimensions, with long-term trust recording a mean of 2.20 and 59.3% expressing disagreement. Regulatory compliance was the only dimension receiving majority approval at 51.4%. Nationalisation was associated with stable employment and social amenities, while 43.2% identified no clear benefits from private or hybrid ownership. Mufulira recorded lower satisfaction than Chingola. The study concludes that outcomes depend on credible contracts, institutional capacity and effective regulation. It recommends mandatory corporate social responsibility, local employment and procurement quotas, and continued ZCCM-IH minority-equity oversight.

title: Eroding operations while elevating innovation: a dual-mechanism model of supplier list disclosure
summary: Purpose Supplier list disclosure has become a defining feature of contemporary supply chain transparency, yet leading firms exhibit strikingly divergent disclosure choices and the empirical literature reports both benefits and costs. Drawing on the relational view and signaling theory, we develop and test a dual-mechanism framework explaining how proactive supplier list disclosure simultaneously erodes operational performance while enhancing innovation performance, and identify the conditions that amplify each effect. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data from Chinese listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we empirically test the relationships between supplier list disclosure and firms' operational and innovation performance. To validate the relational mechanism underlying disclosure's impact on operational performance, we test the moderating roles of supplier concentration and buyer competition. To validate the signaling mechanism underlying disclosure's impact on innovation performance, we test the moderating roles of media coverage and CSR performance. Findings The results suggest supplier list disclosure undermines firms' operational performance but enhances their innovation performance. The negative operational effect is amplified by higher supplier concentration and greater buyer competition, as these conditions increase the criticality and vulnerability of disclosed relational assets. The positive innovation effect is amplified by stronger media coverage and better CSR performance, which improve the visibility and credibility of the disclosure signal. These results are robust across alternative measures, model specifications, and identification strategies. Originality/value Our findings reconcile the longstanding tension between the documented benefits and costs of supply chain transparency by revealing the divergent performance consequences of supplier list disclosure. This study further contributes to the supply chain transparency and buyer-supplier governance literature by identifying key boundary conditions, thereby offering actionable guidance for designing optimal supplier list disclosure strategies.

title: Blockchain-Enabled Industrial Engineering Frameworks for Closed-Loop E-Waste Re Manufacturing: Risk-Aware Optimization, Data Governance, and Social Sustainability.
summary: Rapid technological advancement and shrinking product lifecycles have escalated electronic waste (e-waste) into one of the world's fastest-growing environmental and supply chain challenges. Transitioning from linear "take-make-dispose" models to circular, Closed-Loop Remanufacturing Systems (CLRS) requires precise tracking of product lifecycles, end-of-life (EoL) quality assessment, and transparent multi-stakeholder coordination. This research topic explores integrated, blockchain-enabled industrial engineering frameworks designed to optimize closed-loop e-waste remanufacturing networks. By coupling distributed ledger technology (DLT) with advanced risk-aware optimization, robust data governance protocols, and social sustainability metrics, this framework addresses the triple bottom line of modern circular economies. The focus spans mathematical modeling for uncertainty, secure data-sharing mechanisms across competing entities, and human-centric metrics that safeguard labor rights and social equity throughout the recovery and remanufacturing chain. Key Research Themes & Focus Areas 1. Risk-Aware Optimization & Network Design Dynamic E-Waste Reverse Logistics: Stochastic and robust mathematical models for network design under supply quantity, quality, and timing uncertainties. Risk Mitigation under Volatility: Risk-averse decision models (e.g., Conditional Value-at-Risk) incorporating geopolitical, regulatory, and market disruption risks in secondary raw material supplies. Blockchain-Driven Inventory & Routing: Smart contract-automated inventory control, disassembly scheduling, and dynamic vehicle routing powered by real-time telemetry and ledger verification. 2. Data Governance & Digital Product Passports (DPP) Decentralized Data Architecture: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and federated data structures enabling competitive supply chain partners to share component provenance, maintenance logs, and material toxicity data without exposing proprietary trade secrets. Lifecycle Provenance Tracking: Blockchain-anchored Digital Product Passports tracking electronic components from initial assembly through consumer usage to reverse logistics and remanufacturing. Automated Compliance Verification: Smart contracts for automated audit trails, verifying adherence to global e-waste regulations (e.g., EU WEEE, RoHS, Basel Convention) and carbon credits. 3. Social Sustainability & Human-Centric Systems Fair-Trade E-Waste Recovery: Integration of informal recycling sectors and labor practices into formal, blockchain-verified remanufacturing networks to ensure fair wages, safe working conditions, and occupational safety. Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA): Developing quantifiable metrics for social impacts—community health, worker health and safety, gender equity, and localized economic growth—embedded directly into optimization objectives. Ethical Sourcing & Conflict Material Offset: Ledger mechanisms ensuring remanufactured outputs reduce demand for conflict-mined critical raw materials (e.g., lithium, cobalt, rare earth elements).

title: Beyond the Boardroom: How Diversity and Foreign Ownership Shape Corporate Innovation?
summary: This research examines the impact of board diversity and the moderating effects of foreign ownership on business innovation in DSE-listed manufacturing companies in Bangladesh. The study gathered data from 135 companies across 10 industry groups from 2012 to 2023. Firms’ innovation is proxied by research and development expenditures, whereas board diversity is measured in terms of gender, age, educational qualifications, and experience diversification of the board members. Employing a two-stage least squares method, the study found a positive influence of board diversity on firms’ innovation. The moderating effect of foreign ownership is also significant for firms’ innovation. The study confirms the robustness of the research findings by employing several techniques. The research provides a new perspective for the country, as there is a dearth of knowledge regarding this particular domain and will be helpful in attaining the goal of the SDGs. The practical implications of the study demonstrated that proper guidelines regarding board diversity should be introduced in Bangladesh’s Corporate Governance Guideline 2018.
